questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the denouement in a closing image that reports aftermath rather than outcome
questions.stem: In an amateur astronomer's observing log, an entry closes, 'and by three in the morning the field was empty again, the way a room is empty after everyone has left.' Which part of the story's shape does that closing line perform?

options.text: It resolves the narrator's conflict by stating plainly what finally happened in the field.
options.misconception: treats a lyrical closing as a reported outcome

options.text: It closes the scene by showing the world after the action has stopped, which is where denouement lives.
It starts a new movement, since the empty field suggests another event about to begin.
options.misconception: mistakes an ending for a fresh plot turn

options.text: It explains the earlier trouble so the reader can finally judge whose fault it was.
options.misconception: assumes an ending must deliver an explanation

questions.explanation: The line shows the world after the action rather than reporting a decision, so it settles what the action left behind as denouement does. Reading it as resolution fails because no outcome is stated, and nothing new begins.
questions.hint: Ask what the closing line shows, not what it reports.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an ambiguous ending from an open one using evidence inside the text
questions.stem: One amateur astronomer keeps a log whose final entry ends, 'The light was still there, though I could not say for how long.' Explain why a reader may treat this as an ambiguous ending rather than an open one.

answer.exemplar: An ambiguous ending withholds a verdict while still handing the reader materials to weigh; an open ending simply stops and leaves the reader nothing to work with. Here the closing clause, 'could not say for how long', shows that the writer saw the light and then lost certainty about it, so the uncertainty belongs to the observer rather than to the absence of the text. The earlier entries about waiting on the same object tell the reader what was at stake. Because competing readings remain available, the ending is ambiguous rather than merely unfinished.

questions.explanation: Ambiguous withholds a verdict while still supplying evidence to weigh; an open ending merely stops. The clause 'could not say for how long' makes the uncertainty the observer's, so earlier entries stay open to interpretation.
questions.hint: Distinguish withheld judgement from missing material.

options.text: The crossed-out word proves the entry was copied from elsewhere, so it carries no authority at all.
options.misconception: treats a revision as evidence of forgery

options.text: The revision shows the writer weighing a claim against what the night supported, leaving both readings live.
The revision is a clever trick designed to make later readers overread every other entry.
options.misconception: presumes every ambiguity is a deliberate trick

questions.explanation: Ambiguity the text supports outlasts ambiguity a reader imposes. The revision places two candidate readings in view at once, so the ending stays open, while readings of deception or trickery find no prompt in the log.
questions.hint: Weigh the two readings the writer leaves standing.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a description of place carries the state of the observer
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer opens a log with 'The hill behind the allotments was the colour of a wet slate, and I found that I could not decide whether it depressed me or steadied me.' Explain what the description of the place does to the account of the observer.

answer.exemplar: The description carries the observer's state inside the description of the place, so the hill and the mood cannot be separated. Naming the colour of the hill gives us a scene; naming the effect it had on the writer turns the scene into evidence about the observer. Because the sentence admits two readings of the same view, it also suggests that the writer's judgement is unsettled, which is exactly what a first-person observer's report can reveal. The place is not backdrop but a record of the person doing the looking, and the two cannot be pulled apart without losing something.

questions.explanation: The place is described in terms of its effect on the writer, so the hill becomes evidence about the observer rather than backdrop. Saying the writer could not decide also shows an unsettled judgement, which a neutral description would not.
questions.hint: Notice whose state the description of the place records.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain what comparing two openings reveals that reading them separately does not
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer drafts two openings for the same log: 'The clock in the hall stopped at nine.' and 'The sky that night was the last quiet thing in the county.' Explain how comparing the two openings helps a writer judge them.

answer.exemplar: Comparing openings asks a writer to treat each as a choice rather than as a description, and to ask what each one makes the reader expect. The first centres a domestic interruption that quietly rearranges the evening; the second centres the night as the largest thing available. Set side by side, they reveal that the two sentences are not competing versions of the same atmosphere but different priorities for the entry, and the writer can then decide which priority the rest of the log actually keeps. A comparison also exposes which opening the later pages can support and which they quietly contradict.

questions.explanation: Comparison turns two sentences into two choices, showing what each makes the reader expect and what the rest of the log must then support. Judging them separately as atmospheres hides the real difference, which is the priority each one sets.
questions.hint: Ask what each opening asks the later pages to deliver.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a sentence can leave a reader undecided between two readings
questions.stem: One amateur astronomer ends a log with 'The instrument was steady that night, which I note only because everything else in this account has been unsteady.' Explain how this sentence works to keep a reader undecided.

answer.exemplar: The sentence sets two qualities of the night against each other and makes the steadiness the exception rather than the rule, so the reader is invited to weigh the report against its own context. A reader who takes steadiness as the point of the entry and a reader who takes the long history of unsteadiness as the point can both defend their position from the sentence itself. The claim is not that the text withholds information, since nothing is hidden; it is that the emphasis of the closing sentence points in two directions at once, and the writer lets it stand that way rather than settling which the reader should prefer.

questions.explanation: The sentence makes steadiness an exception inside a run of unsteadiness, so the emphasis points two ways and both readings can be defended. Nothing is hidden here; what is unsettled is which truth the entry is really about.
questions.hint: Ask what the exception makes the rule more important for.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish denouement from resolution in a closing passage
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's log ends its final entry with 'The window was still open, and the room had gone cold by morning.' Explain why this may be read as denouement rather than as resolution.

answer.exemplar: Denouement settles what a story's action has left behind; resolution states how the problem was solved. This closing image shows only the aftermath, an open window and a cold room, with no decision recorded and no outcome explained. The reader is given the shape of the consequences while the business of the plot remains unstated. Because the image contains no verdict on the night that has passed, and because the earlier entries have already described what was observed, the sentence performs the quieting and settling work that belongs at the end of a narrative without pretending to answer anything.

questions.explanation: Denouement settles what the action has left behind, while resolution states how the problem was solved. The image shows only a cold room and an open window, so consequences are given and outcomes withheld.
questions.hint: Separate an outcome from the aftermath of an outcome.

options.text: The description is neutral because the words carry no emotional weight beyond the weather.
options.misconception: denies the emotional charge of the phrasing

options.text: The writer is mocking the reader, since a field that objects to being looked at refuses the log's purpose.
options.misconception: reads a wry phrase as mockery aimed outward

questions.explanation: The field is given an attitude that belongs to the writer's own state, so the description and the mood become one thing. Respect for the land, emotional emptiness, and mockery of the reader each suppose an intention the sentence does not carry.
questions.hint: Ask whose feeling the field is made to carry.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Describe the work a closing paragraph performs in the shape of the account

stimulus.body: Last page of the log, written out fair: The tripod's still outside. I am not going to bring it in tonight. It can stand there until it rusts, for all the difference it makes to anyone.

questions.stem: With the closing paragraph in view, which judgement best describes the closing paragraph?

options.text: It resolves the log by announcing that the observing will continue, however long it takes.
options.misconception: reads a defiant tone as a statement of future plans

options.text: It settles the account by leaving the equipment where it stands and closing on the writer's indifference.
It opens a new stage, since the tripod left outside invites the next entry to begin with it.
options.misconception: mistakes a left-behind object for a plot device

options.text: It comments on the log as a whole, telling the reader what the observer now thinks of the whole enterprise.
options.misconception: confuses a closing gesture with a reflective verdict

questions.explanation: The paragraph leaves the tripod out, declines to bring it in, and closes on indifference, which settles the state of things without announcing a decision or a further stage. Plans, a device for the next entry, and a verdict on the enterprise all add content the text does not have.
questions.hint: Ask what the writer has decided, and what they have not.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Compare two endings that withhold the same interpretation in different ways
questions.stem: One last entry in an astronomer's log ends with the word perhaps and then the writer's indifference to the answer. Another ends with the same clause and the writer's insistence that the question is finished. Comparing the endings, what differs?

options.text: Nothing important; the two endings are the same statement with a different last word.
options.misconception: dismisses a change in what each ending asks of the reader

options.text: The first is ambiguous and the second is open, because the second refuses to say it is the end.
options.misconception: reads a declared ending as an absent one

options.text: The first leaves the question open and still matters to the writer, while the second closes it off.
The first is resigned and the second is satisfied, since indifference and finality read differently.
options.misconception: reads tone as the whole difference between the endings

questions.explanation: Both endings decline to choose between two explanations, but the first keeps the writer's concern alive while the second treats the question as finished. Tone alone, a declared end read as no end, and indifference read as satisfaction each miss what actually differs between them.
questions.hint: Compare what each ending does with the writer's interest in the answer.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Locate the source of ambiguity and judge whether the evidence supports it
questions.stem: One amateur astronomer marks an entry with a note: 'Two readings of this ending are possible and the evidence will not separate them.' What kind of critical judgement is the note making?

options.text: It identifies ambiguity in the text, holding that the evidence supports two readings equally.
It identifies vagueness in the writing, holding that the author lacked a clear intention.
options.misconception: converts a textual ambiguity into authorial confusion

options.text: It identifies a fault in the critic, holding that more careful reading would settle the matter.
options.misconception: locates the uncertainty in the reader instead of the text

options.text: It identifies a puzzle for later readers, holding that the meaning will be recovered in time.
options.misconception: treats ambiguity as a temporary gap in knowledge

questions.explanation: The note locates the ambiguity in the evidence of the text itself and claims the two readings are equally supported. Writer's vagueness, a critic's inadequate reading, and a puzzle awaiting future solutions each move the uncertainty somewhere other than the text.
questions.hint: Ask where the note says the uncertainty lives.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a description of place and a state of mind can be inseparable
questions.stem: One of the log's final sentences reads: the light was a lamp, or a star, or a trick of the eye, and the log does not say. Explain what makes this ending ambiguous rather than a confession of ignorance.

answer.exemplar: A confession of ignorance says that the writer cannot know and leaves the matter there. Here the writer names three candidates and states that the record will not choose between them, which keeps the question alive as part of the text rather than as a gap in the writer's knowledge. Because the candidates differ in kind, one being a physical explanation, one a distant one, and one a fault of perception, a reader can weigh them against the earlier entries. The ambiguity therefore belongs to the log as a document, and the reader is being asked to interpret rather than to sympathise with the writer's uncertainty.

questions.explanation: Naming three candidates and refusing to rank them keeps the question inside the text, whereas ignorance would leave it outside. A reader can weigh them against earlier entries, so the uncertainty is the document's, not merely the writer's.
questions.hint: Distinguish a record that declines to choose from a writer who cannot.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A first line that establishes voice
questions.learningObjective: Read a first line as a claim about the limits of the observer's view
questions.stem: A first line from an astronomer's log reads, 'I could see the whole sky from the gap in the wall, and I could see nothing else.' Which reading of this first line is best supported?

options.text: It establishes a voice of modest self-deprecation, minimising the writer's own opportunity to see.
options.misconception: reads the limitation as an apology

options.text: It establishes a voice that frames vision as narrow and specific, and owns the limits of the view.
It establishes a voice of professional detachment, reporting the state of the site for the record.
options.misconception: reads an owned limitation as detached reporting

options.text: It establishes a voice of complaint, since the gap in the wall is offered as an explanation of failure.
options.misconception: reads a stated limit as a complaint

questions.explanation: The line claims a specific and limited view and does not apologise for it, so the voice is precise about the boundaries of its own seeing. Modesty, professional detachment, and complaint each add an attitude the sentence does not carry.
questions.hint: Ask whether the limitation is confessed, owned, or resented.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Compare two openings that share a figure and differ in what they add to it

stimulus.body: A comparison kept in the back of the notebook. Opening one, from the 1970s book: Tonight the sky was a bad mirror. Opening two, from the 1990s book: Tonight the sky was a good mirror, and I did not like what I saw in it.

questions.stem: A comparison is kept in the back of the notebook between two openings that share a figure. Which comparison of the two openings best holds up?

options.text: The first is darker in tone, and the second is lighter, so they suit different kinds of night.
options.misconception: reduces the comparison to mood

options.text: The second is stronger because it adds an attitude to the metaphor the first one leaves alone.
options.misconception: assumes a more developed line is automatically stronger

options.text: The openings work in opposite ways, since one turns the sky into an instrument and the other into a mirror.
options.misconception: misreads the first metaphor as an instrument

options.text: Both use the same figure, and the second adds a verdict on the reflection the first only implies.

questions.explanation: Both openings share the figure of a mirror, and the second adds a judgement about what the mirror shows that the first leaves implied. Darker versus lighter, added strength, and opposite figures each misdescribe the comparison the notebook records.
questions.hint: Notice what the two openings share before you compare them.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Opening chosen for a stated voice
questions.learningObjective: Compare two declared sequences and what each protects from suspicion
questions.stem: Two rules for opening a log are stated in this item, one protecting the feeling and one protecting the fact. Comparing the two, which claim holds up?

options.text: The two statements are equivalent, since each simply promises truth at the end of the entry.
options.misconception: collapses two different sequences into one promise

options.text: Each states a deliberate sequence and what it is meant to protect from suspicion.
The first is the better method, because facts are more reliable than feelings in a record.
options.misconception: ranks the two methods by reliability

options.text: The second is a trick, since no fact becomes more believable for arriving late in an entry.
options.misconception: calls the second method dishonest rather than deliberate

questions.explanation: Each writer declares an order and names what the order protects: one guards the feeling against distrust, the other guards the fact against doubt. They are not the same promise, and the choice is about method rather than about which is more trustworthy.
questions.hint: Ask what each sequence is designed to protect.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the limits of observation shape a description of place
questions.stem: One village light in an amateur astronomer's description of the sky is the only thing that has a colour. Which aspect of the description most clearly ties the observer to the scene?

options.text: The description is organised around what the observer could distinguish, so seeing shapes the words used.
The description contrasts two kinds of light, which shows the writer's skill in comparison.
options.misconception: reads a comparison as evidence of skill

options.text: The description names a single light source, which makes the account precise and verifiable.
options.misconception: treats a description as documentary detail

options.text: The description isolates the village, which shows how far the writer stands from ordinary life.
options.misconception: infers social distance the sentence does not state

questions.explanation: The sentence is built around the limits of what the writer could pick out, so the language of colour is a product of the seeing. Comparison, documentary precision, and social distance each read significance into details the sentence does not carry.
questions.hint: Ask what governs the choice of the word colour.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a first sentence positions the writer relative to the reader
questions.stem: A line at the head of the log reads, 'Nobody believes me about the halo, and I am tired of arguing.' Explain what this first line does to the reader's position.

answer.exemplar: The opening places the writer inside a disagreement the reader can already hear, and it tells us that the dispute has been going on long enough to exhaust him. That changes how a reader receives what follows: every later claim will be heard as part of an argument already under way, and any detail that could settle it will carry more weight than it would in a fresh report. The line also establishes the tone of weariness, which puts the entry in a long series rather than making it the first word on the subject. A voice is set here less by manner of speaking than by the position the writer occupies in relation to his readers.

questions.explanation: The line places the writer in an argument already under way and exhausted, so later claims are heard as part of a dispute and details that could settle it gain weight. The voice is set by position as much as by manner.
questions.hint: Ask where the writer stands in relation to his reader.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Compare two first lines for what each makes the act of seeing do
questions.stem: Two first lines an amateur astronomer has used before are set side by side: 'The sky was clear tonight, and I saw the galaxy.' and 'Clear tonight. The galaxy, when it came, came sideways.' Which comparison is best supported?

options.text: The second is better, because a sentence with a break in it always holds attention longer.
options.misconception: ranks openings by sentence shape alone

options.text: The first is better, because it names the object before the writer's reaction to it.
options.misconception: assumes a fixed order of naming is always better

options.text: The first names what was seen and then the fact of seeing it, while the second lets the seeing act like the event.
The two are equivalent in effect, because both tell the reader that the galaxy was observed clearly.
options.misconception: ignores the difference in what each line makes happen

questions.explanation: The first line gives the object and then the observation, while the second makes the arriving sight itself the action, which is why it reads sideways. Ranking by sentence shape, insisting on a better order of naming, and calling them equivalent each miss the different effects of the two lines.
questions.hint: Ask what each line makes the act of seeing do.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.learningObjective: Judge the voice a writer declares for a record of observation

stimulus.body: A note pinned to the front of the log: This book is not a record of what I saw. It is a record of how I saw. If you want the sky, look up; if you want me, read on.

questions.stem: Consider the note pinned inside the front cover of the logbook printed here. Which judgement best describes the voice the writer has chosen?

options.text: A voice that makes the act of seeing, not the seen object, the proper subject of the log.
A voice that disowns observation in order to protect the writer from being corrected.
options.misconception: reads a stated preference as evasion

options.text: A voice that invites the reader to distrust every observation recorded in the pages.
options.misconception: inflates a preference into a general distrust

options.text: A voice that is merely informal, since the writer is speaking directly to whoever opens the book.
options.misconception: mistakes direct address for informality

questions.explanation: The note says explicitly that the log records how the writer saw rather than what was seen, so seeing is the subject and the sky is the occasion. Disowning observation, distrusting every entry, and mere informality each misread a clearly stated editorial aim.
questions.hint: Read what the note says the book is a record of.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A first line that establishes voice
questions.learningObjective: Compare a description with its later repetition and judge what the repetition adds
questions.stem: One hill below an observatory is described twice in a log, once as the colour of a bruise, and later with the same words followed by a change. Comparing the two, which claim holds up best?

options.text: The second line cancels the first, because repeating a description revises what the reader should take from it.
options.misconception: assumes repetition cancels an earlier image

options.text: The second line is only a stronger version of the same image, adding force but no new sense.
options.misconception: ignores the new meaning the repetition creates

options.text: The two lines record different hills, since the writer's memory of the place has changed over the years.
options.misconception: invents a change of place the text does not signal

options.text: The second keeps the image and adds a consequence, turning description into evidence about the writer.

questions.explanation: The image is retained and something new is attached to it, so the description becomes the record of a turning point rather than a fresh piece of scenery. Repeating an image does not cancel it, does not merely add force, and does not imply a different hill.
questions.hint: Ask what the repetition adds to the same words.
